correctness.rationale: The proof identifies a unique a^n run for each deletion symbol a, shows it is either destroyed or preserved as the same unique rotation anchor, and reduces equal anchored outputs to the classical same-run linear deletion criterion. Different deleted symbols differ by Parikh content. Exact run counts follow from factors b a^ell c and the q occurrences of a^(n-1); the boundary case n=2 is included. The output probability for a run is ell/q^n. verify.py implements literal deletion and rotation independently and exhaustively verifies all binary cycles through order five, plus 16 q,n FKM cases.

originality.rationale: The exact cyclic one-deletion shadow support and full point-mass spectrum for every de Bruijn circle are not stated by the inspected linear deletion theorems, de Bruijn shift-rule construction, or the published maximum-over-all-necklaces result. These known results supply components but do not imply the special lack of rotation-induced collisions, which requires the per-symbol unique constant-factor anchor. Searches are not proof of priority; an unindexed stronger cyclic-run result remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: Older unindexed cyclic deletion/necklace literature might have the same fixed-source theorem or a stronger anchor lemma.
Run-length distributions of de Bruijn sequences are simple consequences of exact factor counts; novelty rests on the rotation-collision rigidity and complete output law, not these counts alone.
No external independent priority audit has been performed.

value.rationale: A complete and construction-independent output-likelihood law for cyclic universal test sequences is a natural coding/sequence-design invariant. It establishes exactly when quotienting by rotation costs no distinguishability after deletion, despite known nontrivial collapses for arbitrary binary necklaces, and gives the precise run-length-weighted mass spectrum across all alphabet sizes and orders. The theorem is not asserted as a paper-size advance or an optimal code capacity.
